title: Green River Basin Mineral Rights
metaTitle: Sell Green River Basin Mineral Rights (WY)
metaDescription: Minerals under Sublette or Sweetwater County? The Jonah and Pinedale tight-gas fields have paid royalties for two decades. Get a written cash offer.
heroLead: Sublette and Sweetwater counties sit on top of two of the tightest gas plays ever drilled in this country. If your family holds minerals under Jonah or the Pinedale Anticline, we already know the field.
intro: Pinedale is the county seat of Sublette County and gives its name to the Pinedale Anticline, one of the densest gas fields in the Rockies. Rock Springs, the seat of Sweetwater County, sits closer to the southern end of the basin near the Jonah Field. Both fields produce from the Lance and Mesaverde formations, tight sandstone that took modern completion technology to produce economically, which is why a lot of this acreage didn't see real drilling until the 2000s even though the gas had been known about for decades.

Because the pay zones are stacked and the wells are drilled in tight, dense patterns, a single 40 or 80-acre spacing unit here can carry a lot more wellbores than you'd see in a conventional field. That density is good for a mineral owner because more wells means more chances your specific tract is directly under production instead of just near it.

sections.heading: Jonah and Pinedale Aren't the Same Field
paragraphs: Jonah Field sits mostly in Sublette County near the Sweetwater County line and was developed earlier and more densely than Pinedale, with wells spaced as tight as ten acres in the core. Pinedale Anticline covers a larger footprint north of Jonah and has produced for longer, with development continuing on federal leases well into the last several years. Knowing which field, or which edge of which field, your minerals sit in changes the offer, because the two areas have different well counts per section and different remaining reserve estimates.

Operators here have included Ultra Petroleum in the earlier development years, with Jonah Energy, PDC Energy, and Marathon holding significant positions more recently as the fields have traded hands. A change in operator doesn't change your ownership, but it can change how fast division orders get processed and how the royalty statement looks.

sections.heading: Federal Minerals Dominate This Basin
paragraphs: Unlike southern Wyoming's railroad checkerboard, most of the federal minerals in Sublette and Sweetwater counties sit in large contiguous blocks rather than an alternating pattern, because this ground was never part of the Union Pacific land grant corridor. That's actually simpler for a buyer to evaluate in one sense — you're either sitting on private fee minerals or you're not — but it also means a much larger share of the basin's total production runs through BLM-administered leases with federal royalty terms rather than private lease terms.

If your deed traces back to a private mineral reservation that predates the federal leasing here, or you're one of the smaller number of owners holding fee minerals inside these fields, that's a meaningfully different asset than an interest tied to a federal allotment, and we price it accordingly after checking the reservation language.

sections.heading: Tight Gas Decline Behaves Differently Than Shale Oil
paragraphs: Tight gas wells in the Lance and Mesaverde tend to decline steeply in year one, then flatten into a long, shallow tail that can keep paying for fifteen or twenty years at a modest rate. If your royalty checks have dropped sharply from an early peak but have been fairly steady for a few years since, that's the tail behavior, not a sign the well is dying. It changes how we model the remaining value of your interest compared to a fresh horizontal oil well still on its early decline.

Natural gas price swings hit this basin harder than an oil-weighted play, since almost everything produced here is gas with associated liquids. Your royalty check size has probably moved with Henry Hub pricing more than with anything happening at the wellhead, and that's a normal, expected pattern for Green River Basin production, not a red flag.

sections.heading: What We Check Before Making an Offer
paragraphs: Sublette and Sweetwater County records show the deed history, any producing leases, and whether your tract sits inside a currently drilled spacing unit or an undeveloped fringe. We also check BLM lease status where the minerals are federal, since that record shows royalty rate, lease term, and whether the lease is currently held by production.

Send us your legal description or a copy of your deed and a recent division order or royalty statement if you have one, and we'll come back with a written offer that reflects which field, which formation, and which ownership type your minerals actually are.

faqs.question: Is Jonah Field better than Pinedale for mineral value?
faqs.answer: Neither is universally better. Jonah was developed earlier and denser in its core, while Pinedale has a larger footprint with ongoing federal-lease development. We evaluate your specific section rather than the field name alone.

faqs.question: Why did my royalty check drop so much after the first year or two?
faqs.answer: Tight gas wells in this basin decline fast early, then settle into a long, shallow tail. A drop from an early peak followed by steadier payments since is normal decline behavior, not necessarily a failing well.

faqs.question: Are most Green River Basin minerals federal or private?
faqs.answer: A large share of production here runs through federal BLM leases in big contiguous blocks, different from the alternating railroad checkerboard further south. Some tracts are still private fee minerals, and we check the deed history to confirm which you hold.

faqs.question: Does a change in operator affect my ownership?
faqs.answer: No. Ultra Petroleum, Jonah Energy, PDC Energy, and Marathon have all held positions here over time as properties traded. Your ownership stays the same; only the name issuing your division order changes.

faqs.question: My minerals aren't producing yet. Can you still make an offer?
faqs.answer: Yes. Undeveloped tracts near active spacing units in Sublette or Sweetwater County still carry value tied to development trends and lease bonus activity nearby, even before a well is drilled.
